medical.title: Nurse-led program shown to improve midlife dementia risk profiles in new study
medical.summary: New research led by Monash University shows a multi-domain dementia risk reduction program delivered by general practice nurses can improve estimated dementia profiles in middle-aged adults, offering a practical new model for proactive brain health.

medical.title: Plastic tea bags are releasing BPA, plasticizers and up to 2,500 microplastic particles into your cup of tea
medical.summary: Microplastics are now impossible to avoid. They have made their way into everything from agricultural soils to freshwater systems. So, it is unsurprising that they end up in most foods and drinks. However, some methods of packaging or serving these items can increase microplastic exposure even more. One such example is the plastic tea bag. While many tea bags are still made of a cellulose material, some brands use a plastic mesh, despite the well-established fact that plastics can break down in hot water.

medical.title: Many nondrug and nonsurgical therapies for low back pain are more cost-effective than usual care
medical.summary: Nondrug and nonsurgical treatments for low back pain, including psychological support, exercise and self-management strategies, are cost-effective interventions, according to a study published Oct. 27 in the journal PLOS Medicine by Manuela Loureiro Ferreira from the George Institute for Global Health, Australia, and colleagues.

medical.title: Highest endometrial cancer rates found in San Antonio region
medical.summary: An Upper-South region of Texas including San Antonio and Bexar County had the state's highest hysterectomy-corrected incidence of endometrial cancer and the largest increase over time, a study led by scientists at The University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center and the National Cancer Institute showed.

medical.title: Making virtual brain models more biologically realistic by capturing ion exchange
medical.summary: Mean-field models are a powerful tool for understanding collective brain activity. A new model extends this approach by incorporating the exchange of ions between neurons and their surroundings, bringing important biological mechanisms into simulations of neuronal populations.

medical.title: Peptide users don't think of themselves as injecting drug users. Five safety basics injectors need to know
medical.summary: There's a whole new population of injecting drug users. They buy peptides online for muscle building or weight loss, to aid workout recovery or to improve their skin or sleep. Few see themselves as injecting drug users.

medical.title: Switching on healthy silent genes reveals new way to treat Prader-Willi syndrome
medical.summary: WEHI researchers have discovered a way to release a genetic 'brake' that silences healthy genes in Prader-Willi syndrome, opening a potential new path to treating the condition.

medical.title: Public knowledge that alcohol causes cancer rebounds
medical.summary: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans (58%) know that regularly consuming alcohol increases the chances of later developing cancer, according to a nationally representative survey in October by the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC), a statistically significant increase of five percentage points since February 2026.

medical.title: How the body clock could help personalize depression treatment
medical.summary: A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

medical.title: Targeted drug significantly delays advanced breast cancer progression but increases toxicity, phase III trial reports
medical.summary: In a global phase 1 trial, trastuzumab rezetecan showed promising signs of fighting ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer in patients who had already undergone extensive treatment. Also known as HER2-low breast cancer, this subtype is characterized by low levels of HER2, a growth factor protein that can still be targeted for treatment. Trastuzumab rezetecan is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that works like a guided missile, seeking out tumor cells expressing low levels of ERBB2 and delivering a toxic chemotherapy payload directly inside them.

medical.title: It's not (just) the heat, it's the humidity: Examining the impact of intensifying humid heat on pregnancies
medical.summary: New research led by the University of Michigan contains insights for public health officials and communities in Nigeria as they navigate pregnancies through increasing heat and humidity.

medical.title: Comparisons on social media linked to mental health problems
medical.summary: Comparing oneself with others on social media is more strongly associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression among adolescents than using social media to pass the time. This is shown by a study of more than 4,000 Norwegian adolescents, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet in collaboration with the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

medical.title: Health facility data could improve maternal mortality estimates, study shows
medical.summary: Data routinely collected by health facilities could become an additional source for measuring maternal mortality, but the quality needs to improve. Researchers from Karolinska Institutet and Tanzania propose four measures for assessing these data. The work is published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization.

medical.title: Testosterone helps new brain cells survive, but timing matters, study in male rats suggests
medical.summary: Adult neurogenesis is how the adult brain produces new neurons. The newborn cells divide, migrate to specific brain regions and then mature into neurons. Scientists have observed that prolonged testosterone exposure promotes neurogenesis in the adult brain's hippocampus, a region crucial to memory and learning. However, it remains a mystery whether testosterone must act during specific periods of neural development to improve the survival of these new neurons.

medical.title: New leukemia drug suppresses cancer-driving protein more strongly than existing treatments within one week
medical.summary: A more effective and better-tolerated treatment for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) could improve quality of life for people living with the disease. A new study led by Adelaide University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) has provided the first direct evidence that a targeted therapy can rapidly and consistently suppress the molecular signals that drive CML.

medical.title: Are GLP-1s practical and safe for adolescents with obesity?
medical.summary: GLP-1 medications have become a popular tool for weight loss. But are they appropriate for all age groups? Short for glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1s are medications approved by the Food and Drug Administration that treat type 2 diabetes and now obesity. They work by mimicking a natural hormone in the gut that lowers blood sugar, simulates the feeling of fullness and slows digestion.

medical.title: High-dose oxytocin protocol linked to lower postpartum hemorrhage rates
medical.summary: A change in how oxytocin is administered after childbirth may help reduce postpartum hemorrhage, a new study suggests.

medical.title: Brisker walking tied to longer life
medical.summary: In a new study, folks who walked at a brisker pace had a lower risk of an early death. Faster walking speed and more steps per minute are both associated with a lower risk of dying from any cause, researchers report in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Endocrinologists with greater knowledge more likely to prescribe recommended treatment for type 2 diabetes
medical.summary: Endocrinologists who scored highest on the American Board of Internal Medicine's Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) were more likely to prescribe a key diabetes drug class following a treatment guidelines update compared with doctors with lower scores, according to a new study published in JAMA Network Open.

medical.title: Rapid on-site screening could help protect bar staff from hidden drug exposure
medical.summary: The study, published in the Journal of Mass Spectrometry, tested the method in a working U.K. pub and found traces of cocaine and ketamine on surfaces across bathrooms, tables and bar areas.

medical.title: Why every bump in the night feels different: The neuroscience of sensory perception
medical.summary: A haunted house puts the brain on edge. During Halloween, revelers may interpret every creak, whisper or unexpected touch as a sign of something frightening. Safe at home, those same sensations might barely register.

medical.title: Researchers identify the tissue surrounding breast microcalcifications as a key source of diagnostic information
medical.summary: A study performed on 3,504 individual breast microcalcifications (MCs) scanned using high-resolution 3D micro-CT reveals that the surrounding tissue microenvironment provides stronger diagnostic information than the calcified core alone for distinguishing benign from malignant breast lesions. The findings are published in the journal Breast Cancer Research.

medical.title: AI's preference for drugs with a strong online presence may cost millions
medical.summary: Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and Claude, are increasingly being used to provide health information to the public. Although this is beneficial for improving access to treatment information, their limitations were revealed by a new study that found LLMs were biased in their treatment choices and that using these outputs in practice could drive up treatment costs.

medical.title: Faster brain tau buildup linked to faster progression of rare neurological disease
medical.summary: A team of researchers from the National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST) has shown that the speed at which abnormal tau protein accumulates in the brains of people with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is closely linked to how quickly their symptoms worsen. The discovery could help researchers objectively measure disease progression and accelerate the development of treatments for this rare neurological disorder. This study was published in Movement Disorders on Sept. 4, 2026.

medical.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
medical.summary: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

science.title: Embedded enzymes help plastics break down faster in the deep sea
science.summary: Scientists have developed a way for certain types of compostable plastic to break down much faster in marine environments, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea. The breakthrough comes from tiny enzymes embedded in the plastic that help degrade it from within.

science.title: Microscopic springs transform fragile silicon into a flexible terahertz metamaterial
science.summary: Researchers at the Osaka Research Institute of Industrial Science and Technology (ORIST), in collaboration with the University of Osaka and Tohoku University, have developed a flexible and stretchable silicon material whose response to terahertz waves can be mechanically tuned. By etching microscopic spiral springs into silicon, the team made the fragile material bendable and stretchable.

science.title: First light: Hera resolves two asteroids instead of one
science.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft for planetary defense has resolved its two target asteroids separately for the first time, revealing the binary nature of the Didymos system, currently some 197 million km (122 million miles) away from Earth.

science.title: Bonobo females hunt more than males, decade-long study reveals
science.summary: In humans, hunting is considered a man's endeavor. But in one of our closest living relatives, hunting is primarily women's business.

science.title: Does the future of food production start in the lab?
science.summary: Lab-grown protein that mimics the color, taste and texture of meat. Egg white substitutes used for baked goods. Food colorants that replace beta-carotene extracted from carrots. Those are some of the products created with precision fermentation, an emerging technology that can develop tailored food ingredients in the laboratory. If adapted to large-scale production, it can potentially contribute to reducing global food insecurity by creating affordable, sustainable products supplementing those delivered by traditional agriculture.

science.title: NASA’s Neo Surveyor Sunshade
science.summary: A technician inspects the large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor mission in this image released on Oct. 26, 2026. The sunshade structure, which stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base, will keep the infrared space telescope cool as it searches for near-Earth asteroids and […]

science.title: A dinosaur fossil that looks like a mini T. rex just sold for a giant $47 million
science.summary: A dinosaur that looks like a miniature T. rex is now one of the world's most expensive fossils.

science.title: Quantum sensor loop design could improve magnetic measurements for medicine and communications
science.summary: Adelaide University quantum engineers have found a new way to improve some of the world's most sensitive sensors of electromagnetic fields, a breakthrough that could help advance brain imaging, medical diagnostics, communications technology and next-generation quantum devices.

science.title: Metal-free magnetic sensor can be safely implanted for wireless monitoring
science.summary: Researchers in the U.S. and China have created a biocompatible, metal-free magnet that can be safely implanted and generate signals from deep inside the body. Led by Wubin Bai at the University of North Carolina, the team revealed how magnetism can emerge from the rearrangement of atoms in heated carbon nitride, which strengthens the coupling between unpaired electrons.

science.title: New study reveals behavioral shift in southern right whales' selection of nursing sites
science.summary: Australia's southern right whale (Eubalaena australis) population was nearly wiped out by whaling in the 1800s. Since whaling of the species was banned in the 1970s, the number of mother-calf pairs that visit Australia each winter has grown from a few individuals to several hundred.

science.title: Avian influenza threatens vulture populations worldwide
science.summary: Vultures are one of the most threatened groups of birds in the world. Currently, at least 16 of the 23 species of vulture are of conservation concern, largely as a result of poisoning and other threats due to human activity.

science.title: Mapping the green transition of Asia-Pacific economies
science.summary: Countries in the Asia-Pacific can accelerate the shift to clean energy while building competitive local industries as long as policies don't slow access to affordable technologies, a new report has found.

science.title: Human and chimpanzee leaders share a taste for risk
science.summary: People in leadership positions tend to rate themselves as more risk-loving than those without leadership responsibilities—and a similar pattern emerges among chimpanzees: High-ranking individuals are perceived as more risk-taking than their lower-ranking peers. This is the conclusion of a new study by researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Dresden University of Technology, and the University of Portsmouth, published in The Leadership Quarterly.

science.title: GenAI and travel planning: Should AI agents build our itineraries?
science.summary: Whether you're a seasoned tourist or an emerging explorer, delegating travel planning to artificial intelligence (AI) agents is becoming the norm for many travelers.

science.title: Perseverance offers clues to protect crews from ultrafine Mars dust
science.summary: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including particles small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars.

science.title: Election forecasters lack historical data on how national mood drives each senate race, study shows
science.summary: U.S. Senate races are increasingly decided by national forces rather than state-level politics or incumbency advantage. That makes election forecasts less certain than they appear, according to a new study in PS: Political Science & Politics by researchers at the University of California, Davis, and George Mason University.

science.title: How AI planning could create financial market fragility
science.summary: Wharton experts are raising concerns about AI-driven financial market manipulation and runaway technology in a new paper titled "Financial Market Fragility in the Era of AI Planning." Finance professor Winston (Wei) Dou, finance and economics professor Itay Goldstein and Hong Kong University finance professor Yan Ji demonstrate how AI planning technologies could pave the way for collusive trading and increase financial market fragility.

science.title: Earth may have formed much of its water as the planet grew
science.summary: Earth may have produced much of its water during the planet's formation, as rocky pebbles reacted with the hydrogen-rich atmosphere surrounding the young planet, according to new research published in Nature Geoscience. The findings offer a potential explanation for how Earth acquired one of the essential ingredients for life and suggest that similar water-producing processes could be common on rocky planets beyond our solar system.

science.title: Extreme weather drives support for green voting in Europe
science.summary: In representative democracies, it is important that climate change policies are developed through transparent processes and with citizen representation, which in turn requires an understanding of how climate-related events influence public support for such policies.

science.title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
science.summary: Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers.

science.title: The upside of untidiness: Why a little mess can be good for your home
science.summary: If we're to follow the philosophy of organizer extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home.

science.title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
science.summary: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors.

science.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
science.summary: Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.

science.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
science.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.

Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

environment.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
environment.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

environment.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
environment.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

environment.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
environment.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

environment.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
environment.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

environment.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
environment.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

environment.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
environment.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.

mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed a way for certain types of compostable plastic to break down much faster in marine environments, from shallow coastal waters to the deep sea. The breakthrough comes from tiny enzymes embedded in the plastic that help degrade it from within.

mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Osaka Research Institute of Industrial Science and Technology (ORIST), in collaboration with the University of Osaka and Tohoku University, have developed a flexible and stretchable silicon material whose response to terahertz waves can be mechanically tuned. By etching microscopic spiral springs into silicon, the team made the fragile material bendable and stretchable.

mix_items.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft for planetary defense has resolved its two target asteroids separately for the first time, revealing the binary nature of the Didymos system, currently some 197 million km (122 million miles) away from Earth.

mix_items.title: Bonobo females hunt more than males, decade-long study reveals
mix_items.summary: In humans, hunting is considered a man's endeavor. But in one of our closest living relatives, hunting is primarily women's business.

mix_items.title: Plastic tea bags are releasing BPA, plasticizers and up to 2,500 microplastic particles into your cup of tea
mix_items.summary: Microplastics are now impossible to avoid. They have made their way into everything from agricultural soils to freshwater systems. So, it is unsurprising that they end up in most foods and drinks. However, some methods of packaging or serving these items can increase microplastic exposure even more. One such example is the plastic tea bag. While many tea bags are still made of a cellulose material, some brands use a plastic mesh, despite the well-established fact that plastics can break down in hot water.

mix_items.title: Many nondrug and nonsurgical therapies for low back pain are more cost-effective than usual care
mix_items.summary: Nondrug and nonsurgical treatments for low back pain, including psychological support, exercise and self-management strategies, are cost-effective interventions, according to a study published Oct. 27 in the journal PLOS Medicine by Manuela Loureiro Ferreira from the George Institute for Global Health, Australia, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Highest endometrial cancer rates found in San Antonio region
mix_items.summary: An Upper-South region of Texas including San Antonio and Bexar County had the state's highest hysterectomy-corrected incidence of endometrial cancer and the largest increase over time, a study led by scientists at The University of Texas at San Antonio Health Science Center and the National Cancer Institute showed.

mix_items.title: Making virtual brain models more biologically realistic by capturing ion exchange
mix_items.summary: Mean-field models are a powerful tool for understanding collective brain activity. A new model extends this approach by incorporating the exchange of ions between neurons and their surroundings, bringing important biological mechanisms into simulations of neuronal populations.

mix_items.title: Does the future of food production start in the lab?
mix_items.summary: Lab-grown protein that mimics the color, taste and texture of meat. Egg white substitutes used for baked goods. Food colorants that replace beta-carotene extracted from carrots. Those are some of the products created with precision fermentation, an emerging technology that can develop tailored food ingredients in the laboratory. If adapted to large-scale production, it can potentially contribute to reducing global food insecurity by creating affordable, sustainable products supplementing those delivered by traditional agriculture.

mix_items.title: A dinosaur fossil that looks like a mini T. rex just sold for a giant $47 million
mix_items.summary: A dinosaur that looks like a miniature T. rex is now one of the world's most expensive fossils.

mix_items.title: Quantum sensor loop design could improve magnetic measurements for medicine and communications
mix_items.summary: Adelaide University quantum engineers have found a new way to improve some of the world's most sensitive sensors of electromagnetic fields, a breakthrough that could help advance brain imaging, medical diagnostics, communications technology and next-generation quantum devices.

mix_items.title: Peptide users don't think of themselves as injecting drug users. Five safety basics injectors need to know
mix_items.summary: There's a whole new population of injecting drug users. They buy peptides online for muscle building or weight loss, to aid workout recovery or to improve their skin or sleep. Few see themselves as injecting drug users.

mix_items.title: Metal-free magnetic sensor can be safely implanted for wireless monitoring
mix_items.summary: Researchers in the U.S. and China have created a biocompatible, metal-free magnet that can be safely implanted and generate signals from deep inside the body. Led by Wubin Bai at the University of North Carolina, the team revealed how magnetism can emerge from the rearrangement of atoms in heated carbon nitride, which strengthens the coupling between unpaired electrons.

mix_items.title: Switching on healthy silent genes reveals new way to treat Prader-Willi syndrome
mix_items.summary: WEHI researchers have discovered a way to release a genetic 'brake' that silences healthy genes in Prader-Willi syndrome, opening a potential new path to treating the condition.

mix_items.title: New study reveals behavioral shift in southern right whales' selection of nursing sites
mix_items.summary: Australia's southern right whale (Eubalaena australis) population was nearly wiped out by whaling in the 1800s. Since whaling of the species was banned in the 1970s, the number of mother-calf pairs that visit Australia each winter has grown from a few individuals to several hundred.

mix_items.title: Public knowledge that alcohol causes cancer rebounds
mix_items.summary: Nearly 6 in 10 Americans (58%) know that regularly consuming alcohol increases the chances of later developing cancer, according to a nationally representative survey in October by the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC), a statistically significant increase of five percentage points since February 2026.

mix_items.title: Avian influenza threatens vulture populations worldwide
mix_items.summary: Vultures are one of the most threatened groups of birds in the world. Currently, at least 16 of the 23 species of vulture are of conservation concern, largely as a result of poisoning and other threats due to human activity.

mix_items.title: How the body clock could help personalize depression treatment
mix_items.summary: A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

mix_items.title: Mapping the green transition of Asia-Pacific economies
mix_items.summary: Countries in the Asia-Pacific can accelerate the shift to clean energy while building competitive local industries as long as policies don't slow access to affordable technologies, a new report has found.

mix_items.title: Targeted drug significantly delays advanced breast cancer progression but increases toxicity, phase III trial reports
mix_items.summary: In a global phase 1 trial, trastuzumab rezetecan showed promising signs of fighting ERBB2-low metastatic breast cancer in patients who had already undergone extensive treatment. Also known as HER2-low breast cancer, this subtype is characterized by low levels of HER2, a growth factor protein that can still be targeted for treatment. Trastuzumab rezetecan is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) that works like a guided missile, seeking out tumor cells expressing low levels of ERBB2 and delivering a toxic chemotherapy payload directly inside them.

mix_items.title: It's not (just) the heat, it's the humidity: Examining the impact of intensifying humid heat on pregnancies
mix_items.summary: New research led by the University of Michigan contains insights for public health officials and communities in Nigeria as they navigate pregnancies through increasing heat and humidity.

mix_items.title: Human and chimpanzee leaders share a taste for risk
mix_items.summary: People in leadership positions tend to rate themselves as more risk-loving than those without leadership responsibilities—and a similar pattern emerges among chimpanzees: High-ranking individuals are perceived as more risk-taking than their lower-ranking peers. This is the conclusion of a new study by researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Dresden University of Technology, and the University of Portsmouth, published in The Leadership Quarterly.

mix_items.title: Comparisons on social media linked to mental health problems
mix_items.summary: Comparing oneself with others on social media is more strongly associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression among adolescents than using social media to pass the time. This is shown by a study of more than 4,000 Norwegian adolescents, conducted by researchers at Karolinska Institutet in collaboration with the Norwegian Institute of Public Health.

mix_items.title: GenAI and travel planning: Should AI agents build our itineraries?
mix_items.summary: Whether you're a seasoned tourist or an emerging explorer, delegating travel planning to artificial intelligence (AI) agents is becoming the norm for many travelers.

mix_items.title: Health facility data could improve maternal mortality estimates, study shows
mix_items.summary: Data routinely collected by health facilities could become an additional source for measuring maternal mortality, but the quality needs to improve. Researchers from Karolinska Institutet and Tanzania propose four measures for assessing these data. The work is published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization.

mix_items.title: Perseverance offers clues to protect crews from ultrafine Mars dust
mix_items.summary: Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA's Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including particles small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars.

mix_items.title: Election forecasters lack historical data on how national mood drives each senate race, study shows
mix_items.summary: U.S. Senate races are increasingly decided by national forces rather than state-level politics or incumbency advantage. That makes election forecasts less certain than they appear, according to a new study in PS: Political Science & Politics by researchers at the University of California, Davis, and George Mason University.

mix_items.title: How AI planning could create financial market fragility
mix_items.summary: Wharton experts are raising concerns about AI-driven financial market manipulation and runaway technology in a new paper titled "Financial Market Fragility in the Era of AI Planning." Finance professor Winston (Wei) Dou, finance and economics professor Itay Goldstein and Hong Kong University finance professor Yan Ji demonstrate how AI planning technologies could pave the way for collusive trading and increase financial market fragility.

mix_items.title: Testosterone helps new brain cells survive, but timing matters, study in male rats suggests
mix_items.summary: Adult neurogenesis is how the adult brain produces new neurons. The newborn cells divide, migrate to specific brain regions and then mature into neurons. Scientists have observed that prolonged testosterone exposure promotes neurogenesis in the adult brain's hippocampus, a region crucial to memory and learning. However, it remains a mystery whether testosterone must act during specific periods of neural development to improve the survival of these new neurons.

mix_items.title: New leukemia drug suppresses cancer-driving protein more strongly than existing treatments within one week
mix_items.summary: A more effective and better-tolerated treatment for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) could improve quality of life for people living with the disease. A new study led by Adelaide University and the South Australian Health and Medical Research Institute (SAHMRI) has provided the first direct evidence that a targeted therapy can rapidly and consistently suppress the molecular signals that drive CML.

mix_items.title: Earth may have formed much of its water as the planet grew
mix_items.summary: Earth may have produced much of its water during the planet's formation, as rocky pebbles reacted with the hydrogen-rich atmosphere surrounding the young planet, according to new research published in Nature Geoscience. The findings offer a potential explanation for how Earth acquired one of the essential ingredients for life and suggest that similar water-producing processes could be common on rocky planets beyond our solar system.

mix_items.title: Extreme weather drives support for green voting in Europe
mix_items.summary: In representative democracies, it is important that climate change policies are developed through transparent processes and with citizen representation, which in turn requires an understanding of how climate-related events influence public support for such policies.

mix_items.title: 121-million-year-old fossils suggest Longipteryx had no tail feathers
mix_items.summary: Around 121 million years ago, somewhere in modern northeastern China, an early bird took to the skies. If you drew its silhouette, you'd notice something was missing. Unlike any bird alive today, it had no tail feathers.

mix_items.title: Are GLP-1s practical and safe for adolescents with obesity?
mix_items.summary: GLP-1 medications have become a popular tool for weight loss. But are they appropriate for all age groups? Short for glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1s are medications approved by the Food and Drug Administration that treat type 2 diabetes and now obesity. They work by mimicking a natural hormone in the gut that lowers blood sugar, simulates the feeling of fullness and slows digestion.

mix_items.title: High-dose oxytocin protocol linked to lower postpartum hemorrhage rates
mix_items.summary: A change in how oxytocin is administered after childbirth may help reduce postpartum hemorrhage, a new study suggests.

mix_items.title: Brisker walking tied to longer life
mix_items.summary: In a new study, folks who walked at a brisker pace had a lower risk of an early death. Faster walking speed and more steps per minute are both associated with a lower risk of dying from any cause, researchers report in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: The upside of untidiness: Why a little mess can be good for your home
mix_items.summary: If we're to follow the philosophy of organizer extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home.

mix_items.title: Endocrinologists with greater knowledge more likely to prescribe recommended treatment for type 2 diabetes
mix_items.summary: Endocrinologists who scored highest on the American Board of Internal Medicine's Longitudinal Knowledge Assessment (LKA) were more likely to prescribe a key diabetes drug class following a treatment guidelines update compared with doctors with lower scores, according to a new study published in JAMA Network Open.

mix_items.title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
mix_items.summary: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors.

mix_items.title: Rapid on-site screening could help protect bar staff from hidden drug exposure
mix_items.summary: The study, published in the Journal of Mass Spectrometry, tested the method in a working U.K. pub and found traces of cocaine and ketamine on surfaces across bathrooms, tables and bar areas.

mix_items.title: Why every bump in the night feels different: The neuroscience of sensory perception
mix_items.summary: A haunted house puts the brain on edge. During Halloween, revelers may interpret every creak, whisper or unexpected touch as a sign of something frightening. Safe at home, those same sensations might barely register.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify the tissue surrounding breast microcalcifications as a key source of diagnostic information
mix_items.summary: A study performed on 3,504 individual breast microcalcifications (MCs) scanned using high-resolution 3D micro-CT reveals that the surrounding tissue microenvironment provides stronger diagnostic information than the calcified core alone for distinguishing benign from malignant breast lesions. The findings are published in the journal Breast Cancer Research.

mix_items.title: AI's preference for drugs with a strong online presence may cost millions
mix_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT and Claude, are increasingly being used to provide health information to the public. Although this is beneficial for improving access to treatment information, their limitations were revealed by a new study that found LLMs were biased in their treatment choices and that using these outputs in practice could drive up treatment costs.

mix_items.title: Faster brain tau buildup linked to faster progression of rare neurological disease
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers from the National Institutes for Quantum Science and Technology (QST) has shown that the speed at which abnormal tau protein accumulates in the brains of people with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is closely linked to how quickly their symptoms worsen. The discovery could help researchers objectively measure disease progression and accelerate the development of treatments for this rare neurological disorder. This study was published in Movement Disorders on Sept. 4, 2026.

mix_items.title: Governors allied with Flávio Bolsonaro set to lead majority of Brazilian Amazon states
mix_items.summary: Seven of Brazil’s nine Amazonian states are set to be governed by politicians aligned with far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, Lucas Berti reported for Mongabay Brasil. On Oct. 25, Brazil will have an electoral face-off between the top two candidates for several races that were not able to secure more than 50% of the vote in […]

mix_items.title: Inside the ‘unique’ tail of Iran’s spider-tailed horned viper
mix_items.summary: The Iranian spider-tailed horned viper, a rare snake endemic to western Iran, hunts by holding its body completely still while twitching its tail. Its body camouflages among the rocks of its semi-arid Zagros Mountains habitat, but its bulbous tail with accompanying leg-like scales looks remarkably like a large chunky spider. The snake, Pseudocerastes urarachnoides, uses its […]

mix_items.title: As sand becomes more valuable, Sierra Leone’s Mahera Coast grows more vulnerable
mix_items.summary: PORT LOKO, Sierra Leone — When the tide pulls away from the beach in the agricultural regions in Mahera in Lungi, about 27 kilometers (17 miles) across the sea from the country’s capital, Freetown, the digging commences. Young men shovel sand into cement bags and carry them to a flat open area to pile sand […]

mix_items.title: New Zealand builds an arsenal of tools to battle a ‘wily’ invasive seaweed
mix_items.summary: BAY OF ISLANDS, Aotearoa New Zealand — Since an invasive seaweed called caulerpa was discovered in Aotearoa New Zealand in 2021, forming meadows that blanketed parts of the seabed, it’s taken on an almost mythical status among people who spend time in coastal waters. “It’s so wily and so resilient,” Michele Rogalin-Henderson, a doctoral candidate […]

mix_items.title: A study unravels the genetic mystery of a cobra divided by sea
mix_items.summary: COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s spectacled cobra (Naja naja) carries a two-million-year-old genetic mystery, and a new study finds that the island’s cobras form a genetically distinct lineage, reopening a taxonomic question raised by a Sri Lankan zoologist nearly nine decades ago. The study also established that the spectacled cobra has evolved from an African ancestor […]

mix_items.title: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit
mix_items.summary: A surprising two-year clinical trial found that fish oil supplements successfully delivered omega-3s to the brain but failed to improve memory or protect against Alzheimer's-related brain shrinkage. Researchers suspect that getting these nutrients through a healthy diet may offer benefits that supplements alone cannot provide.

mix_items.title: Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.

mix_items.title: Scientists accidentally discover a genetic code that breaks the rules of life
mix_items.summary: Scientists accidentally discovered a microscopic organism with a genetic code that breaks a rule researchers thought was nearly universal. While testing a new DNA sequencing technique, they examined a previously unknown protist collected from a freshwater pond at Oxford University. To their surprise, the organism uses two genetic signals that normally mark the end of a gene to encode two entirely different amino acids instead. These signals were previously thought to evolve together, making the discovery particularly remarkable.

mix_items.title: This “golden tree” coral was too strange for any known family
mix_items.summary: A brilliant yellow coral discovered off Costa Rica proved so unusual that scientists had to create an entirely new family to classify it. The meter-tall colonies rise from seafloors covered in brittle stars, inspiring the Tolkien-inspired name Laurinque elenya, or “golden tree of the stars.” Advanced genetic analysis revealed that the coral belongs to a previously unknown evolutionary lineage.

mix_items.title: Scientists found Homo erectus 200,000 years earlier than expected
mix_items.summary: New fossils from South Africa are reshaping the story of early human evolution. Researchers have described 18 hominin fossils from Drimolen Cave, including an adult Homo erectus skull fragment dated to about 2 million years ago, supporting evidence that the species appeared in southern Africa roughly 200,000 years earlier than long thought. The finds also reveal that Paranthropus robustus, which lived alongside Homo erectus, was gradually evolving even larger teeth and stronger chewing muscles as the climate changed.

mix_items.title: 97-million-year-old fossils reveal the earliest known animal “GPS”
mix_items.summary: Mysterious 97-million-year-old magnetic fossils may be the oldest evidence of an animal using Earth’s magnetic field like a built-in GPS. Their sophisticated magnetic structure could have helped an unknown ocean creature navigate thousands of kilometers with surprising precision.

mix_items.title: One tiny chemical difference between RNA and DNA may help explain how life began
mix_items.summary: Scientists may have found a clue to one of the biggest mysteries surrounding the origin of life: how fragile RNA molecules could gather and survive before cells existed. New research shows that RNA is unusually good at assembling into tiny liquid-like droplets that concentrate molecules and can harden into protective, gel-like structures. Remarkably, much of this behavior may come down to a single oxygen-containing chemical group that RNA has but DNA lacks.
